An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been calculated using data from 10.0 $\text{pb}^{-1}$ of LHCb data from 2010. This measurement, having minimal impact on previous $B^0_s$ lifetime assessments, yields the most precise $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time interval to date, with a value of $0.638 \pm 0.010$ ps. Additionally, this measurement enables a more precise determination of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay width with a value of $(4.0 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-13}\text{ GeV}$ and allows for a search for rare $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays with a branching fraction limit of $(0.8 - 2.4) \times 10^{-6}$. The methodology employed in this measurement serves as a foundation for forthcoming studies of rare $B^0_s\rightarrow f^0(980)K^+$ and $B^0_s\rightarrow $\phi\phi$ decays. The relevance of these findings to the study of rare electroweak corrections is also discussed. The precision of this measurement is reflected in the accompanying figures. This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a specific type of stochastic control problem, known as a distributed regulation problem, using a particular discretization approach. To understand this, we first establish a precise mathematical framework, including the definition of a stochastic evolution equation and the concept of its solution, as well as the formulation of the control problem with the desired outcome of zero. We then examine a discretization method based on the spatial and temporal finite element methods and determine the accuracy of this approach, including the convergence of the solution to the underlying stochastic evolution equation and the optimal control problem. Ultimately, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, both the state and control solution converge to their respective limit values. Additionally, we establish that in the case of a deterministic environment, this discretization approach is equivalent to solving a classical algebraic control problem. Lastly, we provide specific numerical examples to illustrate the application of this discretization approach to real-world problems. Furthermore, we propose a modified version of this method and investigate its performance in a simplified scenario. This research paper relies on the theory of a particular type of stochastic evolution equation known as a monotone linear equation. We believe that the numerical discretization approach presented here can be adapted to other types of stochastic control problems. Lastly, we outline some possible extensions to the research presented here. For the readers convenience, we have included an appendix that provides a derivation of the modified version of the Bensoussan-Lyons-Lasry-Lions algebraic system. We have also included a comparison of our results with the findings of other research papers on the same subject matter. This research paper originated from the PhD thesis defended by the first author in 2020 at the Universite Paul Sabatier in Toulouse, France. The thesis was supervised by the second author. The numerical approach presented in this research paper can be implemented using available finite element software packages such as FreeFem++. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We propose that the energy-driven transformation of the anisotropy patterns may be linked to the transition from a state dominated by the Compton Short Length Scale within the distribution of sources, occurring at this specific energy milestone. We also examine the extent to which local cosmic magnetic field dynamics influence the anisotropy patterns and find that the energy-driven anisotropy patterns may be insensitive to the particular structure of the galaxy they are observed in. We anticipate that the energy-dependent power law and associated energy milestone will serve as valuable inputs for theoretical models seeking to explain the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. The anisotropy patterns exhibited at lower energy levels, although less pronounced, exhibit similar orientations that also support their extragalactic origins, and the segmenting approach highlights local cosmic magnetic field influences on the anisotropy patterns within this energy range. The inclusion of cosmic-ray anisotropy data at lower energy levels, integrated with the recently discovered energy-dependent pattern at higher energy levels, presents a unified anisotropy picture that extends across the entire energy spectrum examined. The comprehensive anisotropy map we present serves as a key observational output that can guide the development of theoretical models aiming to understand the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics across a broad energy range and various galactic structures. The integrated anisotropy data set also facilitates multi-messenger research facilitated by directed searches towards specific cosmic-ray anisotropy patterns and their associated ultra-high energy source candidates detected in the sky. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - solvability. To achieve this proof, it is first established that Zinbiem algebras satisfy the identity of the lower central series, and subsequently, a recursive formula for the (n+1)th power of the lower central series is derived. Ultimately, this leads to the discovery of a chain of invariant polynomials for the adjoint representation of the Lie algebra associated with the Zinbiel algebra, which in turn serves as the basis for demonstrating that the Zinbiel algebra in question is solvable. The paper also explicitly provides this solvability chain in the particular cases of Zinbiel algebras defined over the field of complex numbers or over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Additionally, it is shown that the derived formula for the (n+1)th power of the lower central series generalizes the recursive formula for the (n+1)th power of the upper central series of the Zinbiel algebra, which can serve as the basis for defining the upper central series of the Zinbiel algebra. Furthermore, this generalization is utilized to demonstrate that the Zinbiel algebra satisfies the identity of the upper central series, which in turn serves as the basis for determining its nilpotency degree when defined over the field of complex numbers or over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Unlike previous studies, where missing values aren't considered, we aim to handle missing values, foreign keys, and referential integrity in addition to functional dependencies. We define a set of keys that can identify and distinguish between rows within the table, based on the presence of certain values, foreign keys, and satisfying a set of foreign relationships. We then identify which rows are inconsistent due to missing values, referential breaches, or violating foreign relationships. Our primary goal is to minimize the number of rows deemed inconsistent, while allowing for a flexible interpretation of the data, facilitated by the use of tolerance semantics. We achieve this by selectively applying repairs, which involve adding values to the table, and ignoring certain foreign relationships. Point processes provide a suitable framework for modeling a broad range of data, including frequency counts in time series, network traffic, genetic data, and fluctuations in financial markets. Researchers have extensively explored various point process models, particularly self-exciting processes like the Hawkes process, due to their ability to capture persistent behavior and feedback effects. Despite their versatility, research on point process models has focused primarily on stationary cases, with time-dependent models being less well understood. This study introduces a novel Hawkes process model, with a Poisson-based variation, where the processes' parameters change over time and are estimated using an EM algorithm. A hybrid approach is also developed to speed up computations. Moreover, three different time-dependent scenarios are examined, demonstrating the model's effectiveness. The model's performance is also compared to existing models through numerical experiments and real-world data analysis. The results show that the model's accuracy improves when its parameters are matched to its dynamics, either empirically or theoretically. The study on cancer recurrence data reveals new insights and the model's ability to incorporate external inputs. The model has numerous potential applications, including finance, epidemiology, and genetics. The appendix contains the derivation of the process's conditional intensity equation and its numerical solution. The R code for the simulations and real-data analysis is provided in the SSupplement. The code is also available at the repository https://github.com/abdel1419/TDPA. The research benefits from discussions with Mathieu Cluse and the data provided by Dr. Yves Dumont. The authors are open to collaborating with biologists and epidemiologists to apply the model to new contexts. The model can be generalized to negative feedback by modifying the renewal process component. The model's relationship with the time-dependent self-activated branching process is examined, and its connection to the stationary case, as well as its properties, are established through numerical experiments. The study highlights the model's ability to capture birth-death processes, and the conditions necessary for its stability are defined. The model can be suited for modeling events with a natural upper bound, and the challenges associated with estimating the parameters under these conditions are discussed. The model's potential in neuroscience applications is explored, and its connection to the activity-based models, as well as the advantages it offers over them, are examined. The appendix contains the simulation of the model with the beta process, the numerical solution of the process's conditional intensity equation, and the code for the simulations and real-data analysis. replices both neural descriptor networks and neural relational fields. NDFs
incorporate three key components: a neural network that generates descriptors,
another that identifies a set of reference points on an object, and a third

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes from a 2D space of coupling constants to a 2D space defined by the two independent eigenvalues of the stability matrix of the trivial fixed point. Our calculations yielded that the edge singularity in O(N) universality classes occupies a universal position within this 2D space, fully independent of the model details. Specifically, for a scalar self-coupling model with a symmetry breaking phase transition, we found that the edge singularity lies along the line defined by the coefficient of the $\phi^2$ term being zero, which is bordered by the lines defined by the eigenvalues of the stability matrix equal to zero or the crossover line, respectively. Along this line, the critical behavior is shared with the Ising model in two dimensions. This universal position holds true for all N, and our findings were confirmed through multiple independent approaches. Additionally, our results demonstrated that the edge singularity can be reached by moving in the space of renormalized coupling constants from any self-coupling model through appropriate rescaling, which implies that the universal properties of the Yang-Lee edge singularity are shared by all self-coupling models in two dimensions. Furthermore, our results also enabled us to determine that the edge singularity in the N=1 vector fermion sector is located in the same universality class as the N=1 scalar self-coupling sector, which is consistent with the bulk transfer matrix representation approach. Moreover, our results can be used to interpret the results obtained using the mean field approximation, which is precisely the case for the N=1 vector fermion sector. Lastly, our findings agreed with the predictions made using the bulk transfer matrix representation approach and the d-dimensional cubic lattice bond percolation critical surface in two dimensions. The universal position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity in the 2D space defined by the two independent eigenvalues of the stability matrix of the trivial fixed point provides a concise and intuitive understanding of the Yang-Lee edge singularity and can be used to guide related studies. The findings based on the functional renormalization group can be extended to the edge singularity in Z(2) universality classes in d-dimensional hypercubic lattices. The universal position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity in two dimensions has significant implications for the fundamental issue of determining the non-perturbative definition

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a specific optimization procedure for a particular function can yield a good approximation when using a limited number of data points. The quality of this approximation is often gauged through its distance from the true minimum curvature, a measure that indicates the precision of the approximation. To investigate this further, we examine the results of an optimization algorithm known as the "noise-sensitive AMP." The analysis of this algorithm involves constructing a hypothetical ideal version, referred to as the "Sudakov-Fernique AMP" or SFAMP, which serves as a standard against which the performance of the noisy version is compared. The results of these comparisons are presented as the distance between the two versions, measured as the angle of a specific triangle. The research demonstrates that this angle can be both upper and lower bounded, providing insight into the effectiveness of the noisy AMP. Additionally, by applying these findings to the TAP free energy, we derive an inequality that can be compared with an existing, similar inequality, demonstrating that the two are equivalent. The approach used in this research is unique as it employs the method of averaged marginal posteriors, an analytical tool commonly employed in mathematics and computer science. The results presented in this study can be found in the appendix. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. Furthermore, we carried out observations at the two sites mentioned above to compare the precision of the technique to the standard method used in atmospheric science. According to our analysis, this technique can be precise to a degree of 0.05, however there are areas that need improvement such as analyzing the effects of CCD saturation, the systematic errors associated with the photometric system, and the spectral characteristics of the stars observed. Additionally, we tested this technique on data collected over the course of a year at the two sites mentioned above. Our findings show that this technique can be effective over long periods of time with minimal changes to the system, however there are areas that need further improvement such as analyzing the effects of the system's spectral response, the angular size distribution of the stars observed, and the changes to the system's response due to temperature and humidity. Nonetheless, this technique has the potential to be simple, cost-effective, and can be implemented at existing telescopes with wide-field capabilities. Our proposed method can be further optimized by upgrading to a spectrometer to analyze the spectral characteristics of the stars observed and to upgrade the CCD detectors to more advanced and more precise models. Our team also conducted a feasibility study on using this technique on a space-based platform using the Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer. Our analysis shows that this technique can be effective even in space-based environments with the added benefit of constantly changing star angles and atmospheric scattering. Nonetheless, there are areas that need further improvement such as analyzing the effects of dust emission from the target stars, the system's spectral response, the angular size distribution of the stars observed, and the changes to the system's response due to temperature and humidity. Nonetheless, this technique has the potential to be simple, cost-effective, and can be implemented at any infrared survey

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained popularity, and various methods have achieved high precision. However, this task is challenging and most current solutions have limitations. To enhance pose estimation across the board, researchers introduced the DeepHMap challenge, a benchmark focusing on a specific image scenario with a straightforward background. In this challenge, an object is positioned on a flat surface with minimal occlusion. We investigated possible issues with the existing benchmark and proposed several variations to test robustness and realism. In one version, the background was changed to a complex floor with many obstacles and varying lighting conditions. To tackle this variant, we developed an automatic training pipeline for our network, called DeepHMap++. This network initially separates the image into clusters based on projection dimensions, then learns correspondences between clusters and the 3D object model, and finally estimates the object's pose. With this pipeline, we set and achieved new challenge records on various benchmark variants. Moreover, our proposed network outperformed competing methods on the challenging 3000-image test set. To facilitate further progress, we released DeepHMap++ as an open-source code. The challenge dataset and setup are also open to modification suggestions. The newly created variants are available online at https://github.com/ghristis/DeepHMap-Challenge-Variants. The original challenge and variants were developed for researchers interested in pose estimation, but they can also be useful for other applications in computer vision. The code for DeepHMap++ can be found at https://github.com/ghristis/DeepHMap-Challenge-Solutions. The research was funded by the National Science Foundation under Grant IIS-1916980 and Grant DGE-16172818. The dataset is available for non-commercial use. The challenge variants were created to test robustness and realism in pose estimation and can be used to evaluate and compare different methods. The code for DeepHMap++ is available on GitHub, and the challenge variants are available online. The research was conducted by Ghristis I. V. at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln under the supervision of Prof. R. B. Ashraf. The challenge variants can be downloaded from https://github.com/ghristis/DeepHMap-Challenge-Variants. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address general linear estimation challenges. Building on top of the graphical lasso method, initially developed by Friedman et al., this package provides a flexible framework for a range of applications, including network inference, signal decomposition, and compressed sensing. The algorithm itself leverages quasi-Newton optimization techniques to ensure efficiency and accuracy. Users can easily integrate the package into their existing workflows due to its simple and consistent API. The source code for GGLasso is available on GitHub, along with example use cases to guide users through its capabilities. The package has been tested on large-scale datasets to demonstrate its practical feasibility. The development of the package is ongoing, with opportunities for user contributions and customization. The current version of the package focuses primarily on standard linear models, but future expansions are planned to incorporate non-standard models, such as logistic regression and sparse autoencoders. The package can be installed using pip, the Python package installer, using the command pip install python-gglasso. The documentation for the package is available at https://gglasso.readthedocs.io. The development of the package has been funded by the Human Frontiers Science Program, the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation, and the University of Michigan. The package is open-source, with the source code available at https://github.com/stephane-mandel/python-gglasso. The copyright for the package is held by the University of Michigan. The license for the package is the BSD 3-Clause "BSD 3" License. The package relies heavily on the SciPy and NumPy libraries. The package provides functions for solving linear systems, including the solution to the normal equation, the solution using the Newton conjugate gradient method, and the solution using the preconditioned conjugate gradient method. The package also provides functions for sorting and clustering. The package includes example use cases for compressed sensing, network inference, signal decomposition, and the sparse multivariate autoencoder. The package has applications in neuroscience, genetics, compressed sensing, signal decomposition, machine learning, and genomics. The package has been tested on large datasets, with sizes up to 10,000 samples. The package can handle datasets with missing values. The package includes functions for selecting hyperparameters using Bayesian information criterion, the Akaike information criterion, and cross-validation. The package includes functions for visualizing the results, including the graphical lasso estimate, the reconstructed signal, and the selected network. Numerous biomolecular simulations rely on precise configurations of molecules, often in complex systems with many degrees of freedom.  These simulations frequently solve equations of motion that determine instantaneous molecular movements.  In this work, we present a straightforward method for deriving equations of motion under thermostatting conditions using configurational gradient descent.  This approach is compatible with a variety of thermostatting techniques and provides an intuitive understanding of thermodynamic averaging through stochastic gradient descent.  As a result, this framework is suitable for various sampling strategies, including stochastic configurational integrators, Langevin dynamics, metropolis accept/reject procedures, and more.  By leveraging this method, we developed and tested a range of sampling algorithms, some of which are renowned, while others are novel, to demonstrate its utility.  These simulations involve small molecules moving within nanocrystalline environments and microcanonical molecular dynamics simulations of Tethered Plateaus.  They indicate that the sampling of molecular configurations through stochastic gradient descent can be remarkably efficient.  As an intriguing aside, this framework also enables the derivation of equations related to the Metropolis accept/reject criterion, molecular velocity distributions under equilibrium conditions, and the connection between temperature fluctuations and system temperature.  In total, this work provides a practical and flexible approach for developing and testing a variety of configurational sampling algorithms.  As such, it is suitable for incorporation into general biomolecular simulation frameworks.  In addition to its own merits, this method has the potential to integrate seamlessly with existing simulation tools, making it possible to readily exchange algorithms simply by exchanging code.  As further evidence of this, we successfully integrated one of our novel algorithms, named Vespa, into the GROMACS simulation package, which resulted in a 2.5 times improvement in acceptance ratios for molecular dynamics simulations involving stochastic configurational integrators.  As another example, another novel algorithm, named Sifera, which is related to the SMD method, enabled us to validate the derivations of the Metropolis accept/reject criterion and molecular velocity distributions under equilibrium conditions. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, each node represents an entity connected across multiple relationships, and each layer represents a specific type of connection. We've modified the traditional eigenvector centrality algorithm to account for inter-layer connections and to calculate a centrality measure for each node, taking into consideration both its local influence and its impact across different layers, as well as the relevance of those layers. Unlike current methods that either ignore inter-layer connections or fix the lambda multiplier before calculations, our approach utilizes an iterative method with a flexible lambda value that is calculated as part of the process. This results in a more nuanced measurement that can differentiate centalities across layers of equal importance. We've also developed two variants of this method that allow for further customization. Our research includes comprehensive simulation studies and real-world applications to major universities collaboration networks. The code is publicly available on GitHub. This new method provides a more sophisticated tool for researchers and practitioners to analyze and study multi-layered networks across various fields. The new method can also be applicable to weighted networks by following the suggestions outlined in this study. The proposed method can further be adapted to different research contexts by adjusting the layer weighting scheme. The code for this research can be found at https://github.com/AMMAI/Eigenvector_Centrality_Multilayer_Networks. The current version of the code supports undirected single-layer networks but future updates will include support for weighted networks. The code is written in Python 3.8. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of deriving esophageal tumor boundaries solely from CT scans without using external data, which would make the process more efficient. To achieve this, we developed a system using dense unet architecture with focus and dilated layers to analyze the esophageal region in particular. The system was applied to a dataset from the Society of Computed Body Imaging with specific modifications to better suit the model. The results show a moderate level of accuracy with a score of 0.61 for the DDAUnet model used. To validate the findings, we used a separate dataset from the Medical Imaging Techniques group with separate tubes and air present in the esophagus, which also showed a similar level of accuracy with a score of 0.58 for the DDAUnet model used. The quality of the models was compared and they performed similarly to state-of-the-art models with only a slight difference. Code-mixed languages, which combine two or more languages within the same text, are a key aspect of multilingual societies.  Code-mixing serves as a vital means of communication that transcends language barriers and enables people to convey information that would be lost when translating between languages.  Code-mixed NLP technology holds considerable potential to boost the efficacy of various applications including chatbots, social media analytics, and online content management.  However, developing this technology is a complex task.  Firstly, there is no universally accepted framework for analyzing code-mixed data which varies depending on the languages being mixed and the purpose of the analysis.  Secondly, such data sets are scarce and difficult to obtain due to issues related to data collection, privacy laws, and the time-consuming nature of annotating code-mixed text.  Thirdly, evaluating code-mixed NLP models is a challenging task due to the absence of suitable evaluation metrics.  Fourthly, code-mixed data sets often lack standardization which can hinder comparisons and model transfers.  Fifthly, the vast majority of code-mixed NLP research focuses on languages that are closely related, such as Hindi-English code-mixed data, with little work on more distant language pairs, such as Chinese-Japanese code-mixed data.  Addressing these challenges is crucial to creating practical code-mixed NLP technology that can be used in the diverse multilingual societies around the world.  In this paper, we outline some possible solutions including developing adaptable frameworks for analyzing code-mixed data, creating large-scale high-quality code-mixed data sets, designing suitable evaluation metrics, standardizing code-mixed data sets, and exploring models that can be applied across different language pairs.  We also discuss some related topics including language representation, transfer learning, and sociolinguistic analysis.  We hope this paper will stimulate further discussion and research into code-mixed NLP technology. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that leverages valuable information from multiple sparse domains to enhance the recommendation performance in extremely sparse scenarios. We formulate a multi-task learning model with a carefully designed architecture, incorporating separate modules for handling item and user interactions, which enables the model to effectively capture both global and local aspects of preference. Furthermore, we introduce a novel Strategy-based Item/User Interaction Learning (SIIEL) framework, incorporating a mix of rating-based and recommendation-based strategies to guide the model in identifying the optimal sparse domains for collaboration. We conduct comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR in addressing the challenging sparse-domain cross-recommender task. The code is available at https://github.com/zwang1413/MSDCR. The proposed approach has practical implications for various real-world applications involving sparse-domain cross-recommender challenges. Conic equations are a fundamental aspect of convex optimization and have diverse applications including optimization, control, and statistics. In this work, we provide a type of conic equation that we term 'natural' conic equations and demonstrate how they can be solved using a direct computational approach. This method involves specific and straightforward algebraic transformations that convert these conic equations into an exploitable form where the roots can be determined by examining the concourse of the equation's components. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of unique roots and discuss its relationship with the solvability of a system of natural conic equations. A specialized case of these equations, known as 'diagonal' conic equations, is particularly straightforward and can be solved using an intuitive and graphical method. A Julia package called Hypatia is also introduced which provides an implementation of these methods for solving both individual natural conic equations and systems of diagonal conic equations. This package offers an interactive tool for visualizing the concourse of a diagonal conic equation and systems of diagonal conic equations, and also includes a solver that can be used within other Julia applications. A comparative analysis with established optimization solvers demonstrates that Hypatia achieves superior performance in solving certain systems of diagonal conic equations. A particular application of these conic equations in signal processing is also presented. A comprehensive documentation for Hypatia is available at the package's official webpage. The escalating utilization of magnetic resonance imaging in neuroscience research and clinical applications is driving the need for effective and automated data quality assessment. By enabling the rapid screening of large image datasets, quality assurance algorithms can streamline further analysis for only acceptable data. However, developing such an algorithm is challenging because it requires a high degree of generalization ability to accurately assess images of various types, including those with different sequence weights, head coverage, and pathology severity levels. To address this challenge, we evaluated the sequence-specificity, head coverage generalization, and robustness of several deep learning techniques to the most commonly used MRI brain protocols. Our results showed that even without being trained on specific protocols, a combination of contrast-free and contrast-trained models using a multi-task learning approach demonstrated robust performance across different sequences and head coverage categories. Furthermore, by incorporating a robustness module to the standard scoring function, we found that this setup can handle the variability of protocols with different sequences and head coverage, but its ability to handle tumor protocols derives from the inclusion of contrast-trained models in the training process. Our research also highlighted that the presence of noise in annotation data has a more significant impact on performance than the presence of subjective opinions. To facilitate further advancements in this area, we open-source our code and provide practical guidelines for conducting similar experiments. To accelerate progress, we propose a new research direction: integrating spatial attention mechanisms with patch-based models to enhance performance, especially in the presence of noise and varying tumor protocols. To validate our proposed method, we conducted a series of experiments to examine the influence of noise in annotation data and found that it significantly impairs performance. Moreover, we discovered that tumor protocols pose a particular challenge due to their protean nature. To address this issue, we suggest integrating spatial attention mechanisms with patch-based models to develop a robust quality assessment algorithm capable of handling noise and varying tumor protocols. Our proposed model, named ResUnet, leverages a combination of contrast-free and contrast-trained models using a multi-task learning approach and incorporates a robustness module to the standard scoring function. In a real-world application, we assessed the performance of this model in a clinical setting and found that it can generalize across different sequences and head coverage categories with different protocols. This framework, based on a linear programming dual theory, uses a dual decomposition approach to solve complex problems by subdividing them into manageable sub-problems that can be efficiently solved by individual EV owners. A simulation study, set in the city of Fukuoka with a particular weather pattern, reveals that charging EVs during off-peak hours when demand is low can reduce stress on the distribution network. Furthermore, allowing private EVs to charge during peak hours when they have large batteries available can lead to a 50% decrease in network stress. This study also explores different scenarios with various weather patterns and network configurations to better understand the impact of private EVs on distribution networks across different conditions. It is also proposed that incentives be provided to EV owners with large batteries that can charge during off-peak hours and offer load-shifting services to the grid. With the aim of entering a state of optimal engagement, agents participate in meetings that allow for some level of structure and randomness. Our results show that this state of engagement accelerates learning and problem-solving at both the individual and group levels. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we applied it to a real-world problem - generating characters for the video game The Sims 4. Our findings indicate that this method outperforms existing techniques in various evaluation metrics. To facilitate replication and advancement of this research, we are making the game-based environment and models publicly available. In addition to this, we offer practical guidelines for implementing flow-enhanced multi-agent meetings in various contexts. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Additionally, we explored the effects of lattice parameters on the electronic and magnetic properties of the materials and identified the stable lattice parameters that yield the type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration used in our calculations. Lastly, our findings suggest that materials with the AuCu3 structure hold considerable promise for advanced technological use cases.

This feature has various implications, including in the study of alternating permutation characteristics. Furthermore, it provides the foundation for analyzing the behavior of the number of even elements within a particular cycle type. In fact, it can be an essential tool in examining the generalization of the B2 property from the context of finite classical groups. Specifically, it enables us to generalize the property of B2 in the context of the classical groups SL(n, F) for a given field F, provided that n exceeds the square root of half the size of the field F. In this paper, we also investigate the relationship between the B2 property and the existence of a specific subgroup within the group itself. Additionally, we introduce and examine the generalization of the B2 property in the context of the classical groups Sp(2n, F) for a given field F. Provided that n exceeds the square root of half the size of the field F, we find that the group Sp(2n, F) exhibits the B2 property when n equals 4. A key challenge in kidney sharing networks arises when a patient's immunogenotype doesn't match any available donor kidneys. To maximize transplant opportunities, patients are often prioritized by the number of compatible kidneys they have access to. This study aims to identify the optimal threshold at which a patient with an incompatible kidney should be added to a list in order to increase the number of transplants for others while maximizing their own chances of receiving a compatible kidney. By incorporating stochastic flows and potential reward, we develop a mathematical model to evaluate this decision in varying list sizes and kidney compatibility scenarios. Furthermore, we establish an algorithm to calculate the optimal threshold for a given scenario. When applied to real-world data, this model demonstrates its ability to replicate existing findings and provide new insights, such as the importance of considering waiting lists of other organ types. Expanding the model to account for prioritization based on a patient's expected reward, we observe that a first-come-first-served approach does not always yield optimal results. To accommodate dynamic settings, we explore the inclusion of time-dependent rewards and find that priority should be awarded to patients with the most versatile immunogenotypes. Lastly, we discuss the potential expansion of this model to other kidney sharing networks. This study's findings have implications for the design of optimal algorithms to manage complex transplant networks. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. This issue is particularly pronounced when dealing with proton-proton collision predictions, which can originate from multiple sources, including but not limited to, certain processes with identified hadrons, deep inelastic scattering off external fields, and some heavy flavor productions. To effectively combine these predictions, it is necessary to standardize their structure and component formats. This paper outlines a theoretical framework for collectively analyzing and fitting probability density functions, with a focus on incorporating collision data from particle detectors. To achieve this goal, we develop a comprehensive framework comprising two main components: (1) a set of rules governing the combination of predictions, (2) a numerical tool capable of automating this process. A distinguishing feature of this framework is its ability to combine not only data but also theoretical predictions on probability density functions, based on combined analyses of collision data from detectors. To demonstrate the utility of this framework, we present detailed examples, including but not limited to, processes with identified hadrons, heavy flavor productions, and semi-inclusive scattering off external fields. With this framework, we show that it is possible to reconcile Discrete Ordinacy Approximation and Monte Carlo methods through combined analyses of collision data from detectors. Furthermore, we illustrate the implications of incorporating scattering data off external fields on probability density functions, based on combined analyses of collision data from detectors. To facilitate widespread adoption, this framework is made available to the scientific community through a publicly accessible repository. Consequently, this framework can serve as a foundation for collectively analyzing and fitting probability density functions, with a particular emphasis on incorporating collision data from particle detectors. With its modular design, this framework can be applied to problems both related to but also beyond the scope of this paper. To facilitate further advancements, we outline potential extensions to this framework, including but not limited to, integrating additional collision production processes and heavy flavor productions with hadron colliders. We investigate the connection between a two-dimensional Gaussian free field and multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions (SLEs) in the context of statistical mechanics models. Specifically, we consider a random log-gas model from the beta ensemble with $d$ components and investigate how it relates to $d$ independent SLEs as $d$ approaches infinity. We show that as $\beta$ is set to infinity, one of the SLEs will converge to the chordal SLE with weight $4$, while the remaining $d-1$ SLEs will converge to the radial SLE with weight $2$ for $d>1$. This process occurs over a time scale of $n^2$. We also explore the relationship between the log-gas model and the SLEs in the subcritical regime and identify key parameters that influence whether the SLEs will terminate at the origin or escape to the boundary. Finally, we discuss the differences between the behavior of the uniform ensemble on the circle and the hyperbolic beta ensemble. We investigate the neutrino-induced decay of ultralight dark matter, specifically looking at how it could affect neutrinoless double beta decay and certain cosmological phenomena. Initially, we consider dark matter comprised of scalar or fermion 'photons' with a mass less than $10^{-13}$eV, which would allow neutrinos to interact with dark matter 'photons' due to their oscillations. This interaction could become significant when neutrinos encounter dark matter particles, either in the early universe or in the present day. We examine the implications for neutrinoless double beta decay and certain cosmological phenomena, such as the suppression of neutrino fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background and the overproduction of neutrinos in the early universe. If a non-zero value is observed for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude, it would necessitate a re-evaluation of the neutrino sector based on the decay's energy spectrum. Moreover, we discuss the relationship between this scenario and certain theoretical models, such as axion and scalar fields, and explore the potential for detection through experiments that involve neutrino or dark matter searches. Ultimately, we find that even when assuming a very long decay lifetime, the energy spectrum of the decay products exhibits a distinctive feature that could be exploited in future searches, and we identify a particular window of sensitivity for the future beta decay experiment nEXO-200. Additionally, we provide a straightforward method for incorporating dark matter interactions into neutrino oscillation equations and offer a preliminary estimate of the neutrino oscillation length characterizing this interaction. Lastly, we consider a variant of this scenario in which the interaction between neutrinos and dark matter occurs through a massive force carrier rather than directly, which would result in a significantly shorter neutrino oscillation length and make the energy spectrum's distinctive feature more challenging to detect, but we also identify a potential for detection in this variant. Nevertheless, this variant would likely remain undetected even with an increase in sensitivity in future experiments. Consequently, any detection of the distinctive energy spectrum's feature in beta decay experiments could be followed by searches for the effects of dark matter on neutrino oscillations, which would provide even more information about the neutrino sector. If the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude is found to be zero, it would allow for a lower bound on the dark matter particle mass, which could range from $10^{-14}$ to $10^{-12}$eV, and would also imply that the energy spectrum's distinctive feature is unlikely to be detected in beta decay experiments. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar-mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within fixed intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that the distribution of recurrence intervals between neutron star binaries' outbursts is not, in fact, concentrated around a specific range. Instead, it trends towards longer intervals as the systems' average wait times increase. As a result, we expect at least some of the long-interval quiescent X-ray binaries in the Milky Way's center to actually be neutron star binaries rather than black holes. In fact, if we assume the majority of these sources have similar properties, then approximately 70% of the long-interval quiescent X-ray binaries in the center should be comprised of neutron stars. This study arrived at this conclusion based solely on observational data, without considering any theoretical black hole properties. It was able to achieve this result without referencing any specific population models, and it utilized the complete sample of known low-mass X-ray binaries in the Milky Way's center. In the context of the black hole vs. neutron star debate, this finding can be verified through continued observational efforts, such as detecting more outbursts from known sources or identifying specific optical counterparts among the known variables. If a neutron star is found among the long-interval variables, then it's likely that at least some of the black hole candidates will actually be neutron stars as well. On the other hand, if no recurring outbursts are found from any of these sources, then it's possible that all of the black hole candidates will actually be black holes. If we assume that the majority of the long-interval variables are indeed neutron stars, then it's worth noting that the shortest possible recurrence interval for which we have evidence is around 6.4 years. This information, coupled with the known minimum wait times for low-mass X-ray binaries, suggests that the majority of the variables in the Milky Way's center have masses below 1.5 solar masses. This research demonstrates that thermal motion causes fluctuations in the geometric structure, leading to time-dependent Poincaré-Houssier effects in polyatomic molecules. This phenomenon results in oscillations between different quantum states, driven by the thermal motion of atoms within the molecule. Furthermore, this finding highlights the importance of incorporating the dynamics of electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions in materials science, chemistry, and biology. When creating neural conversational agents, we face a problem that arises from the diverse goals users may have when interacting with these systems. One possible approach to addressing this challenge is to use Natural Language Inference (NLI) as a performance measure, as it assesses a model's ability to capture the semantic variations users may exhibit during a conversation. We propose a method for evaluating the NLI performance of conversational models, incorporating a mixture of supervised NLI tasks and semantic-related user feedback. We also explore two issues related to NLI evaluation: the presence of "borderline cases," which may confuse the models, and the variety of semantic relationships, which can be difficult to model with limited data. We conduct experiments using a newly created NLI dataset for which the variety of semantic relationships is controlled, and find that constrasting NLI tasks using NLI vectors yields the best performance. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of this approach in a simulated conversation setting. We make the newly created NLI dataset, called Dialogue NLI, available to the public. The occurrence of sustained rotations in low-mass stars is thought to be a critical factor in their internal and external behavior, especially in the context of hydrogen burning. Computer simulations demonstrate that low-mass stars with substantial rotational energy can maintain rotation-induced internal heat through thermal irradiation at their surfaces, and that this effect hinders the development of convection in these stars. Notably, this phenomenon prevails even when these stars are rotating close to their maximum possible speed. Recently, locomotion through contact interactions has been successfully achieved with humanoid robots using hybrid methods that combine foot and hand contacts. However, there are several reasons why bipedal robots might prefer hybrid locomotion. Firstly, hand-thrusters could be used to provide additional propulsion, making hybrid locomotion more efficient than pure bipedal motion. Secondly, having more degrees of freedom in the locomotion task can significantly reduce the required torque and increase stability. In this work, we present a comprehensive approach for controlling a four-legged robot using hand-thrusters to modulate its center of mass trajectory during locomotion. We start by developing an analytical model to understand the dynamics of a simplified four-legged robot. Then, we utilize the nonlinear model to create a closed-loop state feedback controller that ensures stable operation and optimizes the thruster forces. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of different thruster forces on the robot's dynamics and validate our approach through simulations and physical experiments using a hexapod robot equipped with hand-thrusters. In the simulations, we observe that the controller reduces the robot's oscillations and promotes stable locomotion at higher speeds. Additionally, the experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using hand-thrusters to propel a physical robot at various speeds, with the recorded results reflecting the observed trends. In the simulations and experiments, we also explore the potential benefits of hand-thrusters on a bipedal robot and propose several possible configurations for such a setup. Lastly, we conclude by outlining potential applications and future research avenues for thruster-supported bipedal locomotion. The approach presented in this work can be applied to other robots with similar dynamics, and we make our code available online for further development. The current code includes simulations with a hexapod robot, but it can be modified to accommodate other robot configurations. The approach we took in this work is also related to other control methods that involve hybrid zero dynamics and backstepping, and it can be combined with these methods for even better performance. We create a higher-level framework by integrating valued domains with a total residue map and a group scheme over a base field $k$. This integrated framework is referred to as a valued group scheme. Valued group schemes possess a natural valuation, and we establish that it is extensible to a valuation on the quotient field of a domain obtained by localizing its associated domain. Furthermore, we discover that valued group schemes are equivalent to certain types of group-like objects defined using divisorial valuations. Building on this discovery, we establish that divisorial valuations can be characterized as the non-trivial extension of a specific valued group scheme. Additionally, we find that the property of a domain having property $R$ is equivalent to the property of its associated domain being integrally closed. This domain property is then utilized to provide a more general proof for the fact that domains with property $R$ are indeed catenary. Finally, we offer an alternative and more elementary proof for the fact that the normalization of a domain with property $R$ is also catenary. This latter result was previously established by using the properties of the Krull spectrum. Moreover, we provide an example of a domain with property $R$ that is not strongly catenary, and also demonstrate how valued group schemes can be used to generalize and refine the results of Heier and Koch. Lastly, we conclude by investigating the behavior of valued group schemes under the process of extending valuation. This process is utilized to generalize and obtain more explicit expressions, as well as to recover and generalize results already established in the literature. This includes recovering the previously established fact that the normalization of a domain with property $R$ is also catenary. As energy efficiency continues to top the list of priorities for mobile devices, a new challenge emerges at higher performance levels, where speed begins to surpass energy savings benefits. This paper introduces a novel, performance-energy optimization problem aimed at finding the most energy-efficient CPU frequency below a given throughput threshold within a mobile application's execution timeframe. We develop a precise mathematical representation of this problem and leverage convex optimization techniques to create an effective solution method. To validate our approach, we employ real workload data and observe an average frequency reduction of 30% with minimal performance degradation. Furthermore, our approach can be integrated into existing mobile operating system frequency scaling mechanisms with minimal modifications, offering a simple and lightweight solution. Ultimately, our research demonstrates a promising path for exploring a previously unexamined area of CPU frequency optimization. We open-source our research framework, known as HyperDegrade, to the mobile research community.

Neural language models have significantly outperformed $N$-gram models in recent years but suffer from the challenge of low resource settings. We investigate neural models' limitations by conducting experiments using the Residual Learning framework, which leverages the strong performance of neural models while exploring the potential for $N$-gram models to learn from them in low data scenarios. Our results show that neural models can be modified to learn $N$-gram models from their parameters, and this residual learning yields $N$-gram models with improved performance. Furthermore, we discover that using KNearest Neighbors as the sampling method allows for the transfer of linguistic knowledge from neural models to $N$-gram models with a single example. We achieve state-of-the-art performance in the tiny domain adaptation task and apply our residual learning to the Wikipedia link prediction task, yielding comparable performance to the current baseline models. Moreover, our proposed framework is cost-effective as it utilizes existing pre-trained neural models without the need for additional training. As expected, there are no significant improvements when working with ample data sets. We open source our code and data preprocessing procedures for public use.

In an inflationary cosmos, a specific scenario where scalar perturbations cause premature collapse of the scalar field potential can result in the formation of black holes. We investigate the conditions under which this phenomenon occurs within the inflationary scenario based on the $\alpha$-attractor model using both slow-roll and preheating theories. Specifically, we examine how the model's parameters influence the formation of black holes and explore the potential for this effect to be observable in the power spectrum of scalar perturbations. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between this phenomenon and preheating dynamics, including both oscillatory and oscillation-dominated regimes. In the oscillation-dominated regime, we find that the probability of black hole formation becomes negligible. In the oscillatory regime, we identify the location of the sound horizon at the time of preheating mode formation as a critical factor influencing black hole formation probabilities. In this regime, we also determine the characteristic scales associated with both the scalar field's harmonic oscillations and the breakdown of the disturbance at specific multipole moments, and demonstrate how these scales compare to the Hubble radius during Hubble expansion. Finally, we outline the potential for this effect to be distinguishable through future observations, including the use of multi-field $\alpha$-attractor inflation as a model. This integrated framework consists of four key components: a background removal module to preprocess the images, a character segmentation module to split the images into individual characters, a classification module to identify the characters, and a verification module to confirm the accuracy of the results. This paper delves into the specifics of overfitting in linear models with a large number of parameters, analyzes how it relates to the eigenvalues of the data covariance matrix, and provides explicit conditions for non-degenerate, self-renewing, and large eigenvalue scenarios. This study explores a decentralized approach to managing energy storage in multi-period markets with uncertainty and production constraints. Distinguishable players with limited storage capacity participate in spot markets to optimize their self-interest, despite the presence of system-level constraints such as balanced supply and demand. Using stochastic fluid models, we identify risk-averse players' optimal self-allocation strategies for medium-scale networks. Interestingly, we find that risk-averse players exhibit similar behavior to those prone to model uncertainty, with storage serving as a buffer to protect against demand shocks. Furthermore, we determine the optimal storage size and risk-averse parameter values that minimize expected costs under various network configurations. Empirical analysis based on real data highlights the practical implications of our findings. This study contributes methodologically by integrating stochastic fluid models with entropy-based risk measures and provides actionable advice for independent energy storage operators.

In this work, we explore the potential capabilities of Hamiltonian Neural Networks in deriving gradients, which are essential components for backpropagation. Current implementations of HNNs primarily focus on optimizing synthetic objectives, but we suggest a novel method to learn the Hamiltonian dynamics underlying neural networks by utilizing gradient information. This approach enables the hamiltonians to be transferred across tasks and networks of varying sizes. Through comprehensive experiments, we validate the proposed method and demonstrate that learned hamiltonians can successfully approximate the underlying dynamics, even when the network size differs. Furthermore, we showcase that pre-trained hamiltonians can be effectively adapted for new tasks, specifically optimizing cost functions that involve derivatives. To evaluate the proposed method in a real-world setting, we apply it to a subset of the MNIST dataset and discover that learned hamiltonians can be successfully transferred and fine-tuned to achieve comparable performance to standard optimization techniques. Lastly, we discuss the limitations of HNNs and potential avenues for expansion. Code is available at https://github.com/ghale/hnn-learning-derivatives.

This proposed framework enables the development of robust learning models by addressing issues like bias and inaccuracies. We also present a practical application of this framework to traffic forecasting, a problem that interests many researchers and has numerous practical uses. In this example, we use simple learning models to demonstrate how the proposed framework can be effective in forecasting traffic accurately. To evaluate this proposed framework further, we conducted additional experiments with more complex learning models. Our research shows that the proposed framework can improve the performance of learning models consistently. In the end, we outline possible avenues for expanding this proposed framework into more intricate scenarios. Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically using BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with many current methods incorporating a glossary of word senses as context, which enhances the model's performance.  However, these methods generally assume that the provided glossary accurately reflects the relevant context, thus not utilizing contextual information effectively.  We hypothesize that incorporating contextual information into WSD tasks can yield better results.  To test this hypothesis, we developed a simple yet effective approach called Context-gloss, which integrates contextual information with the glossary.  Our results show that Context-gloss outperforms the current state-of-the-art in several evaluation metrics, demonstrating the significance of incorporating contextual information in WSD.  Furthermore, we discovered that incorporating glossary information into the context can also lead to substantial performance gains, with Context-gloss exhibiting particular success in distinguishing between senses with similar definitions.  To ensure the reproducibility of our results, we open-sourced our code for the Context-gloss model.  Lastly, we identified three senses with similar definitions that can serve as future research topics.  Our approach can be applied to other Senses Tagging tasks, which involve tagging the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings based on the provided text.  One such task is the Sense Tagging in Question Answering, which can benefit from our Context-gloss model.  With the advancement of pre-trained language models, the difficulty in obtaining large datasets with annotated glossaries poses a challenge for evaluating WSD models.  One such dataset is the Sense Tagging in Question Answering, which can be used to evaluate models in this manner.  Another such dataset is the SemEval-2010 Task 7, which consists of news articles with annotated word senses.  However, this dataset has several limitations, including a small sample size, with only 200 instances, and only includes senses for the word "election".  To overcome these limitations, we propose creating a large dataset with annotated glossaries, which we call the Context-gloss Election Dataset.  This new dataset consists of over 5,000 election-related articles from Wikipedia with annotated word senses, along with a set of pre-computed semantic features.  We also developed a simple yet effective evaluation method for WSD models, which compares the predicted senses with the annotated senses.  One such evaluation method is the SemEval-2010 Task 7

This study focuses on key-partner databases in cross-domain text-to-SQL tasks, where a primary database serves as the central source of information, while the partner databases hold secondary, supporting information. To achieve this, we employ a dual-table setting with a primary table and an auxiliary table that is not part of the standard SQL syntax. Furthermore, the auxiliary table allows for the incorporation of external knowledge through a proxy table. In this approach, the auxiliary table is used to guide the model's attention towards relevant information, both within the primary database and in the external knowledge. This is demonstrated through an application to the SchemaLink dataset, where Wikipedia serves as the auxiliary knowledge. The results show that incorporating external knowledge through the auxiliary table leads to a 5.08% improvement in exact set matching and 7.96% in a relaxed version. Additionally, the model's performance is compared to a system that incorporates external knowledge through a separate text-to-table model, demonstrating the effectiveness of this end-to-end approach. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work requires close examination is in the field of politics. Political journalists often share the same generic job description, yet their specific tasks can vary greatly. Despite this, few studies have compared the ways in which Web search results, shaped by algorithms that favour popular and up-to-date information, influence political versus non-political journalists. This study's primary objective is to investigate whether there's a noticeable difference in how Web search results affect journalistic work among political versus non-political professionals. We conducted an experiment involving 150 journalists, half of whom worked in politics and the other half in non-political fields. They were presented with a set of search results, some of which were designed to mimic the kind of information often overlooked by Web search algorithms. The study reveals that, indeed, there is a notable discrepancy between how political and non-political journalists work with the information they're given, and how they handle the kind of information Web search algorithms tend to ignore. Moreover, our findings suggest that political journalists are more prone to focusing on widely accepted facts and tend to overlook the kind of information considered'sensational' or 'unverified'. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing strategies and innovative variations. Although such methods ensure the preservation of certain properties, they often fall short in meeting two essential requirements for solving large-scale problems: employing efficient time-stepping schemes and developing effective iterative solvers for large systems of equations. This study addresses this gap by introducing efficient and flexible Krylov-based solvers that preserve key properties, leveraging the flexibility of the underlying time-stepping schemes for sparse systems. A special focus is given to implementing these solvers within existing software frameworks. A comprehensive set of numerical experiments is presented to demonstrate the practical advantages of these methods. This study specifically explores the application of Krylov-based solvers to preserve the non-negative aspect of solutions in one-dimensional conservation laws, but the proposed framework can be extended to other spatial dimensions and other property-preserving contexts. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a challenge. We estimate the accuracy of real-world datasets to be around 90% relative to a fully supervised flow estimation method. Our proposed framework is competitive when combined with the best self-supervised and supervised flow estimation methods, as validated through rigorous ablation studies. We additionally explore the practical applications of our method in real-world settings, demonstrating the value of motion trajectory data derived from self-supervised flow estimation for object classification and as a crucial safety-related feature for obstacle detection. We open-source our code and datasets for public use. The newly introduced benchmark datasets can be found at https://github.com/PRM-TU-Darmstadt/3D-Scene-Flow-Benchmark, the code at https://github.com/PRM-TU-Darmstadt/3D-Scene-Flow-Benchmark-Code, and the 3D flow estimation challenge at https://prm.tu-darmstadt.de/3D-Scene-Flow-Challenge.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call policy learning within containerized microservices. During operation, Timeloops automatically determines the system calls a service should be permitted to make and prevents unauthorized calls from being made. In addition, it learns policies from observed system calls and combines them with security guidelines based on workload categories. If a breach occurs, it can detect the issue and adapt policies accordingly. If a similar scenario occurs in the future, it can recall the previous policy to prevent similar security incidents from happening again. Our research shows that using workload categories and system call histories as security guidelines results in a 50% reduction in false positives when comparing it to using workload categories alone. Furthermore, in comparison to a manual system call permission management approach, it reduces administrative workload by the same margin. Our findings are supported by experimental data obtained from real-world deployments of Timeloops. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome.  Since the games are often settled in the final stages, tactics may need a second look.  Research so far primarily focuses on possession-based metrics and tends to value draw results over wins.  To tackle this issue, we used deep reinforcement learning to create an enhanced action value function that places different values on various game stages based on if the team is leading, trailing, or drawing.  To evaluate this new metric, we compared it to existing methods using real soccer game data.  It shows not only a more significant discrepancy between winning and drawing results than traditional methods but also the actions that lead to wins are substantially different from those that lead to draws.  This finding aligns with general soccer coach knowledge.  Furthermore, we discovered leading teams tend to conserve their lead rather than press for more, while trailing teams tend to press harder for more goals.  This urgency to score increases as the game nears its end.  This research contributes a new action evaluation framework that can be used to train AI soccer players and even offers insights for human coaches on the complex dynamics of soccer games.  It also highlights the importance of distinguishing between winning and drawing results in the metrics used to evaluate tactics.  To take it a step further, we trained an AI player using this new framework within a simulated soccer game environment, and as expected, it prioritized wins over draws.  To validate this finding, we conducted additional experiments under different game settings, which showed that AI players trained with this new framework tend to develop different tactics than those trained with the original method.  This new framework can be used with any existing reinforcement learning algorithms, not just deep reinforcement learning.  It is also scalable and efficient, which is crucial for real-time applications like live soccer games.
