Our study aims to clarify the underlying mechanisms influencing hadron elliptic flow in heavy-ion collisions by examining whether event shape characteristics play a significant role. To this end, we investigated how the $\langle p_t \rangle$ and $v_2$ of inclusive particles correlate with each other in three different ways: (1) examining if there's a consistent power law between them, (2) analyzing if both averages demonstrate similar sensitivity to transverse momentum, and (3) investigating the relationship between their anisotropy components using a 4-particle cumulant method. Our findings are based on Pb-Pb collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy and reveal that the answers to these questions depend on whether we consider charged pions, kaons, or protons. For example, while both averages exhibit a power-law correlation, proton and kaon distributions exhibit distinct sensitivity to transverse momentum, whereas charged pion distributions behave in a similar manner. Additionally, we observed that the anisotropy components of both averages converge when considering 4-particle cumulants. Our research suggests that hadron elliptic flow is influenced by multiple factors, including initial conditions and fluid dynamical properties, and that event shape characteristics play a significant role in this process. Nevertheless, we found that hadron mass also exhibits a significant influence on this process. Our study utilized ALICE collision data at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.

We established that the GDoF gain from optimal power control over binary power control can be extremely large, scaling polynomially at the extremes, but we also found that in many-fan-in scenarios, this gain can reach any speed, greater than linear, up to polynomial scales, by employing an approximation technique that uncovers the underlying principles and demonstrates the availability of networks exhibiting an arbitrarily large category of GDoF gain speeds. Furthermore, we discovered the exact scaling ($\sqrt{K}$) of the GDoF gain from optimal power control over binary power control in networks with a specific structure, namely those with an irregular many-to-few-in structure. We believe this precise result holds for all network configurations but couldn't be proven generally. Lastly, we explored the optimal power control policies and binary power control configurations and derived their general GDoF characteristics. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, existing models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration method utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated its accuracy by comparing the results to experiments involving single air bubble collisions with a spherical particle. Our method was then integrated into a simulation of a rotating tank filled with air bubbles and glass particles, and the results were found to be accurate when compared to similar experiments conducted at the same Reynolds number. Our method has the potential to significantly reduce computational costs while maintaining high precision in particle collision simulations. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Our simulation data is also publicly available on the CFD Cluster. Our research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant Nos. 11732008, 12072244) and the Science and Technology Ministry of China (Grant No. 2018-GF-02-3013-0430). Our research collaboration involved interactions with experimental data from the University of Michigan and the Delft University of Technology. Our method has the potential applications in simulating complex flows with multiple colliding particles in various industries. Our simulation of a rotating tank filled with air bubbles and glass particles led to several interesting observations, including the formation of a particle-rich layer near the tank wall, the creation of vortices and bubble collisions that shape the distribution of particles and air bubbles. Our simulation results can be used to validate our method and provide accurate, experimentally-verified data for industrial flows involving multiple colliding particles. Our method involves integrating our multiple-time-step integration method with open-source flow simulation software, OpenFOE, and our particle collision simulation software, PFC3D. Our simulation results match experimental data when the Reynolds number is low, however at higher Reynolds numbers our simulation results differ from the experimental data, possibly due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, the inability to precisely model the collision time step, or the need for higher precision in calculating the fluid flow around particles. Our research highlighted the challenges in accurately simulating particle collisions and flow interactions at high Reynolds numbers, and the limitations of current models in precisely calculating collision time steps and fluid flow

This article presents an innovative approach to solving the Diophantine equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ where both $a$ and $b$ are whole numbers. By applying a quadratic transformation, we obtain two distinct equations: $64c^2-1=7d^2$ and $(2c)^2 \pm (2d)b \pm (2c)^2 =7^n$. Leveraging existing results on the first equation, we can establish constraints on the solutions for the second equation, ultimately leading to the conclusion that there are no solutions for $n \le 9$. Furthermore, we derive an upper bound for possible solutions of the second equation in terms of $n$, which can be refined to $(n+3)/2$ when $n$ is even. Combining these findings with those from the literature, we are able to state that the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ has no whole number solutions for $n \le 9$ and any solution for $n \ge 10$ must satisfy $n \le (323+14\sqrt7)/2$. Lastly, we provide examples validating the given upper bound for $n=10$ and $n=11$. For $n \ge 12$, we have solutions for $n=12, 14, 16, 17, 18$ and the corresponding values are given. Additionally, we offer a constructive approach to finding solutions for the second equation, enabling us to generate solutions for the original equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ when $n$ is an odd number greater than 3 and can be expressed as $n=4k+3$ for some integer $k$. This allows us to express solutions for any odd $n$ in a particular format. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of ground reaction forces and the lack of clear boundaries between different terrain types. A primary obstacle in tackling this problem is the difficulty in modeling ground reaction forces when the ground is subject to large deformations. In response to this challenge, a widespread approach has been to overestimate the amount of ground penetration by assuming the ground to be stiff, which can lead to conservative estimates of forces and potentially hazardous situations. To address this issue, this work assumes the ground is easily deformed and models ground reaction forces using a comprehensive approach that accounts for force-dependent terrain properties. This method enables force estimation through simulation, although it complicates the control of leg forces. To tackle this complication, a control strategy that corrects forces based on previous force estimates was developed. As a result, this approach can safely estimate forces on a variety of grounds, from soft soils to muddy surfaces. Furthermore, force predictions can be used to update the state of the ground, allowing for further generalization to different terrain types. To validate this approach, it was applied to a hopping monopod simulator, and the results showed that it accurately predicted forces on different grounds and efficiently updated the state of the ground with force feedback. Lastly, this approach has been made available as an open-source tool for researchers to use in their own simulations. In the future, integrating this approach with vision-based ground state estimation holds significant potential for safely navigating various ground environments. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the inherent structure of the underlying data network. Presently, most techniques represent networks as flat graphs, disregarding the inherent taxonomic relationships between their concepts. As a result, existing algorithms often produce markups that are difficult to understand and don't reflect the original context. In this work, we argue that network structures should be represented using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to effectively capture the inherent taxonomy. We then present a scalable method for automatically constructing DAG-based hierarchies from relational data and evaluate it using real-world datasets. The results show that our approach outperforms existing techniques in various scalability metrics. We also explore the relationship between our method's performance and different network density characteristics and contribute a new definition to this field. The research is demonstrated through tangible examples and visualized output. The code developed during this project is available as an open-source contribution. The ongoing work involves refining the method to handle noisy data and determining the optimal graph representation to ensure the scalability and accuracy of the hierarchy generation process. The research is applicable to various domains, including but not limited to knowledge graphs, semantic web technology, and social network analysis. Quantum annealing technology holds promise for efficiently solving complex combinatorial optimization problems by leveraging interactions between their classical and quantum components. Despite this potential, the quantum annealing interval required for successful solution finding often needs significant adjustment, as it's highly sensitive to the particular instance being solved and typically determined heuristically. This research introduces the quantum annealing interval's relationship to quench dynamics in quantum annealing, revealing that during a quench, driven by an increasing transverse field, dynamical phase transitions occur that mirror the quantum phase transition of the corresponding Hamiltonian. As a result, finding the optimal quantum annealing schedule allows for determination of the ideal interval for successful solution finding, equivalent to tracing the quench dynamics through the quantum annealing protocol. This understanding is demonstrated using the exact cover problem, for which the ideal interval is recovered by analyzing the quench dynamics through quantum phase transition characterization tools. This research provides a universal and problem-independent framework for efficiently adjusting the quantum annealing interval in the exact cover problem. As such, it offers a practical solution for this and likely many other problems. As a result, researchers can now find the ideal quantum annealing interval simply by conducting a single simulation of the quench dynamics in the corresponding Hamiltonian, following which the optimal interval is obtained through direct analysis of the resulting dynamics. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Furthermore, this finding has practical applications, enabling us to classify all harmonic functions that decay at a polynomial rate on these manifolds and providing a convenient alternative to an earlier result proved using an established growth estimate. Lastly, this research also explores the concept of Liouville theorem for a related type of manifold where the scalar curvature is bounded rather than constant, and includes an estimate of the dimension of the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on this type of manifold.

We investigated how variations in the gravitational parameter $\gamma$ affect parallax measurements in a post-Newtonian framework, with the aim of placing $\gamma$ within the range acceptable by general relativity using Gaia-like astrometric data as an example. By considering only relativistic effects and ignoring systematic errors in observations, we found that even in a mission with high precision similar to Gaia, the uncertainty in $\gamma$ remains largely unchanged at about 0.0005. Although this estimate originates from a model based on Gaia's characteristics, it's likely to be applicable to any mission with a similar measurement technique. Consequently, we expect future missions with even smaller error bars to retain essentially the same $\gamma$ uncertainty as Gaia. Notably, this prediction holds true for missions using the same technique despite their greater observational accuracy. It's worth mentioning that the predicted value holds under the assumption that the measurement of the celestial reference frame remains accurate. If this is not the case, then any possible error in the measurement of this frame could lead to a much larger value for $\gamma$ uncertainty. For instance, overestimating the solar parallax by 0.002 would result in a value for $\gamma$ close to 0.1, which is far from general relativity's predicted value. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven approach, involving two key steps to address open-domain Commonsense Question Answering. Firstly, we incorporate a coarse knowledge retrieval phase to gather a vast amount of knowledge, followed by a careful selection phase to pinpoint precise, relevant information. To achieve this, we develop a unique strategy that leverages graph-based semantic representations to ensure the retrieved knowledge shares similar characteristics with existing question contexts. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation metric, along with a suite of previously established benchmarks, to assess our approach. In comparative trials, our method demonstrates superior performance in both precise and lenient evaluations. To ensure reproducibility, we make available pre-trained models, along with instruction guides, to facilitate easy replication of our results. Despite the underlying complexity of S-TOP, our method showcases promising efficacy, paving the way for further refinements and enhancements. Astronomical environments are susceptible to modifying the spectral signatures of molecular ions, which are abundant in space.  While comet spectra are primarily analyzed using molecular cation spectra, knowledge of how these spectra are modified is limited.  A review of available data reveals that comet spectra are likely missing spectral signatures of the most abundant molecular cations, which are oxygen-based.  To enhance the comprehension of comet spectra and identify missing spectral features, this review emphasizes the importance of further research into the composite spectra of these molecular cations.  Combining theoretical and observational approaches is crucial for accurately interpreting the chemical composition of comets and similar celestial bodies.  Theoretical predictions of combined spectral features for the most abundant oxygen-based molecular cations are presented, along with the modifications of their individual spectral features, which are likely affected by solar ultraviolet radiation, interstellar radiation, and low-temperature effects. The inclusion of laboratory data from cometary analogues, such as meteorites and asteroids, is also proposed as a means of extending the applicability of this research to these celestial bodies. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  Research indicates that among incarcerated adults in the United States, roughly 25% possess some form of mental health condition, with a third of those with a disorder being severe enough to cause significant functional impairment.  Despite the prevalence of mental health issues within this population, required mental health treatment within prisons is not universally implemented, and its effectiveness is not well understood.  Using a quasi-experimental design based on a change in law, we find that court-ordered mental health treatment for individuals convicted of felonies leads to a 37 percent decrease in symptoms of depression and anxiety two years after release from prison.  These results hold for a variety of subgroups, including those with more severe mental health conditions, those who have prior convictions, and those serving longer sentences.  We also examine the potential mechanisms underlying these results and find that treatment during and after release from prison is associated with improved mental health outcomes.  Finally, we discuss the policy implications of our findings for designing effective post-release services and improving community reentry programs within the criminal justice system.  Ultimately, our research highlights the effectiveness of required mental health treatment for reducing mental health disorders among former inmates and suggests that mandating treatment can be an important tool for reducing recidivism and improving overall well-being. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses that challenge by presenting a new regularization technique, consistent regularization, which enhances semi-supervised medical image segmentation using minimal annotations. A small set of annotated images and large unannotated databases are used to train a consistent representation, as measured by segmentation performance on previously seen scans. This representation is then fine-tuned using the sparse annotated data. Experiments with lung and colon segmentation demonstrate consistent results across two datasets, showing that our method outperforms existing semi-supervised models when enough annotated data is available but requires careful tuning to perform better than existing methods with limited annotated data. Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's solver team introduced a simple text-based format for representing constraints within SMT solvers. This standard, now widely adopted, has undergone significant evolution, and we have observed its potential benefits in various settings. Building upon this foundation, we present the Alethe project, which aims to further refine this format for solving theorem-proving problems. We have tested this new framework on a diverse set of problems and problems from the TPTP repository, and the results show that it can be just as effective as veriT for solving these issues. Moreover, to demonstrate the versatility of this standard, we have incorporated it into the Coq proof assistant by using the SMT interface and the Z3 solver with the Alethe format, and the results indicate that it can be as efficient as using veriT via this same interface. Furthermore, we have explored the possibility of using this standard in a more sophisticated way, including the integration of context-dependent constraints, and the results from a limited set of tests suggest that it can be effective in these scenarios. Lastly, we have made the Alethe project's source code available to the public domain under the BSD license. In line with the workshop traditions, the paper that follows provides a more in-depth examination of the Alethe project.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The observed characteristics also offer a contrasting perspective to the generally prevailing rapid galaxy evolution in similar weak interaction scenarios. The dark matter distribution in UGC 8839 is further investigated through the rotation curve analysis, with the addition of a specific "cored" profile to the standard model, which is widely accepted but requires refinement. The results are compared to other similar weak interactions and theoretical predictions from $\Lambda$CDM simulations. Offline learning for multiple agents interacting in complex environments poses a
significant challenge, as the number of relevant data points is often much smaller
than the number of possible state-action combinations. This issue is exacerbated
by the need for a central controller to consider the diverse actions taken by
multiple agents. To address this, we propose a method that focuses on learning
from high-frequency actions that have been observed in the offline dataset and
have been associated with positive outcomes. This approach is efficient because
it reduces the search space for the controller by limiting consideration to
actions observed in the data that have been linked to desirable results. As a
result, a value-based method is used to establish a connection between these
high-frequency actions and their associated values. This connection serves as
the target for the controller to maximize. To enable this targeting, a policy
is learned that matches the behaviour observed in the data, with high-frequency
actions being treated as the environment's responses to the controller's actions.
This allows for a natural connection between the observed actions and their
associated values. To evaluate this approach, we compared it to existing offline
multi-agent methods using challenging datasets created with diverse reward functions. 
The results show that our proposed method outperforms the competition in scenarios
with small to medium-sized datasets.

In this program, researchers use a combination of algebraic and geometric techniques to analyze and understand complex systems and their relationships. In the course of our investigation, we also identified a particular subset of conformal field theories that demonstrate a particularly strong and curved behavior in response to change, which we referred to as "convex theories." These theories stand in contrast to the "cyclic theories" that we identified earlier, which instead of behaving in a curved and strong manner, behave in a more fragile and weak manner. Utilities like electric companies typically acquire auxiliary services like energy storage to complement their primary services.  The value of these services is influenced by the market in which they're used, requiring utilities to have forecasting capabilities.  Despite this, there's a lack of research on forecasting the value of auxiliary services.  This study develops a novel approach, the Auxiliary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM), which forecasts the value of energy storage.  ASAM incorporates factors like storage capacity and market variables including renewable generation forecasts.  Testing ASAM against actual data showed it outperformed traditional methods.  One of the model's advantages is its ability to provide actionable insights for policymakers.  For instance, it can identify optimal pay-for-performance schemes that increase storage value.  This study found that performance-based incentives that pay more for high renewable generation days can increase storage value by $12 to $18 per kilowatt.  This research has been applied in practice by a major electric company in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States.  As renewable energy integration continues to grow, understanding the value of energy storage and how to design effective policies to encourage its use will become even more critical. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to investigate range-based supervision as an efficient method for resilient convolutional neural networks. In this project, we employed activation clipping with a commonly used neural network and tested it against existing resilient methods with both synthetic error and actual memory defects in various vision tasks including MNIST, Leukemia detection with Pap, and a self-driving scenario with the Cityscapes dataset. The results show that activation clipping can compete with more complex resilient methods, offering a significant decrease in memory usage with comparable accuracy. In late October 2019, student-led demonstrations broke out in Chile, primarily focusing on education reform but soon escalating into widespread protests and riots across the country.  This project aims to adapt and expand a mathematical model originally developed to represent university student behavior during the 2009 Italian protest events.  The existing model accounted for both local and global infection dynamics and included a critical "latent" phase, and we have modified it to incorporate factors specifically relevant to the Chilean protests.  A numerical solution to the model equations was obtained and compared to available data on protest participation, revealing some inconsistencies.  However, issues of over-parametrization became apparent, and several model components were found to be unnecessary.  A simplified two-phase model was then derived and found to match the observed protest data trends fairly well.  This model highlights the significance of both local interaction and global influence on behavior as well as the protests' impact on their surrounding environment.  It also provides numerical evidence for the existence of a critical point where the model's basic reproduction number equals one, which may be related to the decline in protests seen around mid-November 2009.  This finding suggests that the decrease in protests during that period may not have been caused by government intervention but rather natural seasonal variation.  A similar analysis was conducted for the Chilean protests but was limited to the model's local dynamics due to data availability constraints.  This research also explored the protests' impact on their surrounding environment using a more specialized "footprint" metric and found it to be relatively stable over time.  This stability is consistent with the protests' ongoing and widespread nature as opposed to a concentrated and transient event.  This research provides a starting point for further modeling extensions that could account for the protests' dynamic distribution and "footprint" changes over time. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Collection (FSC) challenge, a significant issue that arises during the amalgamation of diverse web-based data sources, including, but not limited to, knowledge networks, tabular data, and spreadsheets, where certain entries can conflict with each other. To address this challenge, we need a set of high-priority records that are universally accepted and can be efficiently gathered from dispersed data sources without the need for access to the underlying data, only the collected network knowledge. After presenting the FSC problem's theoretical framework and discussing related work, we formally define high-priority record extraction as a significant issue and present a straightforward, non-parametric approach to solve it. Additionally, we provide a more advanced solution using a model that includes a prior distribution over the data sources. Both methods are subsequently evaluated through realistic synthetic and real-world experiments. Finally, we outline a research trajectory for tackling the complex aspects of the FSC challenge. A discussion on the challenges and our proposed solutions' implications for the research community can be found in Section 7. All algorithmic implementation codes are available at https://github.com/ghthink/FSC.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations in silicon, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying decoherence sources in quantum devices and propagating terahertz waves in nanoscale environments. This research also explores a vector calibration technique for near-field terahertz measurements, essential for extracting material properties from scanned data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique for analyzing both static and dynamic terahertz effects in quantum devices. This study's findings are relevant to a broad range of nanoscale materials and quantum technologies that rely on terahertz waves and near-field terahertz microscopy. This research is an outcome of discussions held at the workshop "Terahertz Quantum Information Processing and Near-field Terahertz Microscopy and Spectroscopy" organized by the Terahertz Quantum Information Technology Thematic Network. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a specific type of plasma-based component, where a magnetized plasma with a specific geometry is used to alter the polarization of laser pulses, while also increasing their intensity. Simulations demonstrate that a circularly polarized laser pulse can alter its polarization from circular to linear, with a significant increase in intensity, and that this component can withstand terawatt laser pulses. Additionally, simulations indicate that this component can effectively convert a linear laser pulse to a circular one with enhanced intensity, and that this process is resilient to variations in plasma density and magnetic field strength. This proposed component has the potential to enhance the capabilities of advanced laser systems, and can be interpreted as a theoretical model for metamaterials used in laser pulse interaction studies. Moreover, this work provides valuable insights into the nonlinear optical responses of plasma-based and magnetized plasma components, offering promising avenues for developing sophisticated laser pulse manipulation tools.

By treating the tau's mass as a variable, we have obtained a more nuanced understanding of the ratio's dependence on the tau's mass and energy scales. When fixing the tau's mass to its physical value, we have determined the ratio of the tau's electric dipole moment to its charge by combining our form factor calculations with data on the tau's decay into two photons and deriving the relevant hadronic matrix element from the same data. This approach has allowed us to determine this ratio both in conformal QCD and in the presence of collinear QCD. Notably, we have found that the ratio of the tau's electric dipole moment to its charge is independent of energy scales in conformal QCD. In contrast, when incorporating the effects of the tau's mass and the relevant data on the tau's decay into two photons and electrons, we have identified the ratio of the tau's electric dipole moment to its charge as a function of the energy scales influencing the tau's mass and the hadronic matrix element extracted from the same data. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As such, this method allows for the treatment of dynamic processes where the distribution of matter and energy varies over time, with no a priori constraints on the eigenmodes of oscillation. We have successfully tested our method against existing results for nonrotating stars, as well as against the integral relations derived under certain simplifying assumptions, with excellent agreement. Furthermore, we have utilized this approach in modeling the thermal evolution of rotating stars, with particular reference to red giant stars undergoing mergers. This has involved solving the radiative diffusion equation over time, with results compared to existing models. With this approach, we have achieved equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity, with applications in the study of massive star evolution, particularly in the context of binary mergers and asymmetric supernova explosions. This has also allowed for the investigation of thermal and chemical stratification in stellar mergers, with particular reference to giant stars. With this method, we have simulated the thermal and chemical evolution of red giant stars undergoing mergers, with resulting outcomes compared to observed stellar populations. This approach has the potential for further enhancement with the addition of magnetic and mass loss effects, among other processes, with the aim of advancing our understanding of rotating stars in the context of binary mergers and asymptotic giant branch stellar evolution. This has implications for the distribution of nickel-56 produced in supernovae, with particular reference to the electron capture process in the thermally unstable branch of massive stars. This may also shed light on the origins of the metal poor stars in the Milky Way, with particular reference to the chemical composition of the stars in the halo of the galaxy. This has further implications for the distribution of matter in the galaxy, with particular reference to the distribution of dark matter, as well as the formation and evolution of the metal poor stars in the galaxy. This may also provide insights into the origins of the massive star mergers that give rise to binary neutron star mergers, with particular reference to the neutron star neutron star merger.

This paper presents an automatic labeling method to create high-quality training data for extracting specific information from varied documents. It employs a style transfer technique to generate new documents with only the relevant information after removing superfluous content from existing documents. However, this approach requires a substantial amount of computation to create a sizable dataset with diverse documents. To make document extraction models more practical for real-world use, we developed an efficient documentation on using this method to produce a limited amount of high-quality labeled data. Moreover, we introduce a novel evaluation metric that compares the effectiveness of generated documents in a different manner than typical metrics. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we created a dataset called "News Digest," consisting of documents with information on stock market updates. It outperforms existing publicly available datasets with regards to diversity, complexity, and simplicity. Furthermore, we show that document extraction models can be trained using just 100 labeled documents from the News Digest dataset, with only a 10% improvement in accuracy compared to models trained on the existing public datasets. Nevertheless, this method has the potential to significantly reduce labeling costs by as much as 99%. To facilitate reproducibility, we made the code and generated News Digest dataset available for public access.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches utilizing matched filters have been employed but have limitations in handling parameterized signals effectively. This paper presents a novel application of a deep learning model to achieve this goal. We developed a convolutional neural network that effectively distinguishes binary neutron star, binary black hole, and neutron star-black hole mergers based on their gravitational wave signals. The network's efficiency in distinguishing these mergers is indicated by high accuracy rates, with results showing that it outperforms traditional approaches. This model has been optimized for real-time analysis on a laptop. Furthermore, we demonstrate the possibility of inferring the mass of the black hole in binary black hole and neutron star-black hole mergers directly from the gravitational wave signals alone. This achievement has implications for reducing the parameter space of neutron star-black hole events for electromagnetic follow-up analysis. The code for this research is publicly accessible on GitHub. This model has the potential to contribute to enhanced electromagnetic detection of compact binary mergers and provide insights into the properties of dense matter. This finding highlights the capabilities of deep learning in gravitational physics and the potential for similar analyses of other compact binary merger events. Urban settings are known to benefit physical and mental health through public interactions in cities, but COVID-19-related precautions have significantly reduced these encounters. This study used a vast dataset of over one million observations of urban behavior in three major cities, captured before and during the pandemic, to examine the impact of COVID-19 on urban interactions and their connection to individual characteristics. It was discovered that visitors to public spaces decreased substantially, with a notable decline in low-income diversities. Furthermore, low-income diversities plummeted during peak pandemic periods, with declines of 42-64% in different cities. Consequently, the already limited access to diverse urban experiences for low-income individuals has been even more severely restricted, exacerbating existing social inequalities. Moreover, low-income individuals' reduced access to diverse urban experiences may have lasting effects, leading to increased social isolation and accelerated mental health deterioration. Consequently, urban planners and policymakers must prioritize measures to enhance public interaction safety protocols to address these growing concerns. Additionally, strategies are needed to increase low-income individuals' access to diverse urban experiences, thereby mitigating the adverse effects of the pandemic on already marginalized populations. The massive protostar, YL, was discovered with a 0.86 pc diameter and a mass of approximately 87 solar masses, making it one of the most massive protostars known. By analyzing its spectral lines, researchers were able to determine that YL is primarily composed of hydrogen, with small amounts of helium and heavier elements. A comparison with other massive protostars reveals that YL has a similar temperature (57K) but lower total luminosity (1.5x10^4 solar luminosities) and a significantly smaller molecular envelope (approximately 0.07 solar masses). Unlike other massive protostars, YL lacks a disk, and its molecular envelope is primarily made up of 13C, with an abnormal 13C/12C ratio that is twice as high as in the sun. This ratio suggests that the material in YL's envelope originated from massive, short-lived stars rather than massive supernovae. Additionally, the presence of 16O-rich cores within YL's molecular envelope indicates that it formed through the accumulation of material over time, rather than forming instantly. This theory is further supported by the presence of dense cores with varying masses, including some with masses similar to that of the sun, and the presence of outflows that are directed radially, suggesting that the material accumulated over a long period of time before being dislodged by radial convection. This process likely took tens of thousands of years and allowed for the formation of a massive star through mergers of low-mass cores rather than just accumulated material. This conclusion is also consistent with simulations of protostar formation, which show that massive stars can form through the merger of low-mass cores rather than just accumulated material. This research on YL provides valuable insights into the formation of massive stars and highlights the importance of mergers in its formation. This is also consistent with observations of young star clusters that show that massive stars are often found at their centers, which could be the result of multiple mergers. This theory is further supported by the presence of binary and multiple star systems that can also lead to mergers, and the fact that low-mass cores can also contribute to the formation of massive stars through the process of stellar evolution, either directly or through the formation of compact remnant stars. This research on YL also highlights the importance of observing star clusters over time to observe the formation and destruction of low-mass cores and the mergers that occur within them. This research investigates how a uniform current affects nonlinear surface waves in a layer of deep water. Unlike similar studies that examine the effects of a constant current on water waves in a shallow water environment, the present work focuses on the long-wavelength regime of deep water. By assuming that the surface elevation varies slowly across the water, we apply the Hamiltonian approach to derive an equation describing the evolution of these long-wavelength water waves with a constant circulation. In order to achieve this, representations of the environment's structure and layout are crucial for informing decisions.  Despite the potential benefits of using spatial representations, they are often overlooked in practice due to the high costs associated with their construction and updating.  This paper presents a novel method for automatically generating and continuously updating spatial representations, specifically hierarchical topological maps.  These maps integrate the benefits of topological maps with the precision of grid maps, enabling seamless integration with existing navigation systems.  Through simulation testing, HiTMap has demonstrated superior performance compared to non-hierarchical models in navigating in unknown environments.  Furthermore, HiTMap has been deployed on a real robot to test its capabilities in a complex, dynamic outdoor setting, with promising results showing a notable increase in navigation accuracy.  The code for HiTMap is available open-source on GitHub.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging when using object-based programming models due to inefficiencies in memory management, primarily resulting from fragmented memory. To address this limitation, researchers have traditionally employed array-based programming, forsaking the benefits of object-based programming, including safety and memory protection. In response to the expanding use of SIMD devices in critical applications, such as aerospace, where reliability is paramount, there's a renewed interest in object-based programming. This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed to automate memory management on SIMD devices. By automatically configuring itself based on performance and reliability requirements, DynaSOAr achieves a balance between memory fragmentation and performance. Moreover, DynaSOAr features a predictive alignment module that boosts performance by minimizing memory alignment overhead and a block-based allocator that enables efficient memory pooling. As a result, DynaSOAr exhibits superior performance and lower overhead compared to existing manual and automatic memory management approaches. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's design enables secure multi-threading in object-based programming, facilitating applications with complex data structures. To validate DynaSOAr's effectiveness, this research includes extensive performance evaluations and comparative analyses, in addition to case studies involving real-world applications, including a critical aerospace simulation tool. Consequently, DynaSOAr is now part of the Open Source ROCS Framework under the Apache License.

Our analysis highlights the presence of undesirable effects when using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding the noise encountered in simulations.  Qudits introduce unnecessary complexity and we demonstrate that qutrits are no improvement over qubits due to a specific dimensional expansion phenomenon.  In particular, we show that d-dimensional systems inevitably introduce extraneous noise terms proportional to (d-2).  As a result, d must be set significantly higher than 2 in simulations.  To achieve reliable results with qutrits, we establish that d should be at least 8.  Furthermore, we observe that noise in sQED simulations is primarily systematic rather than stochastic. Our findings show that, due to polarization radiation, the positrons emitted by a thick target become highly polarized - with a polarization factor of 0.57 for a carbon target. This degree of polarization is remarkably resistant to changes in the intensity of the laser. In fact, the polarization remains significant, exceeding 0.4 for a wide range of densities, spanning from very low densities to extremely high densities characteristic of solid and liquid states. This extremely high polarization degree, coupled with the efficiency of positron production in thick targets, makes polarized positrons readily available, with a density rate that exceeds $10^{12}$ per steradian for a carbon target. Given a positive integer $k$, a group $G$ is classified as a $k$-width group if its generating series relative to the standard basis has degree $k$. We establish that only trivial groups possess a linear width property within the realm of finite groups. Moreover, we demonstrate that groups possessing a specific polynomial width can be achieved through a variety of constructions, thereby enabling the generation of a diverse range of $k$-width groups. Specifically, our research yields methods for generating $k$-width groups arising from the combination of a $k$-width Coxeter group, the bilinear extension of a $k$-width dihedral group, or the addition of a specific set of group elements. Our results also implicitly provide an alternative proof for the fact that there is an integer $k$ such that any finite group can be represented as a $k$-width group. The study of group widths can be viewed as a part of the broader context concerned with the examination of exponential generating series associated with combinatorial structures. We offer an expansion of our research to this more extensive framework, thereby enabling an understanding to be gained about the properties of certain combinatorial structures, as well as providing an alternative, group-theoretic interpretation of the concept of width $k$. These fields, also known as Gelfand-Tikhonov regularizers, are widely used in inverse problems with Riemannian manifolds and have important applications, especially when working with geophysical or astronomical datasets that require spherical representations. Since these fields often result from optimization methods, their statistical properties can be evaluated by analyzing the statistics of the noise that they reach equilibrium with. We show that the mean and covariance of these fields in equilibrium with additive Gaussian noise on a sphere are given by one-step prediction equations under certain conditions and demonstrate the validity of these results through numerical examples using synthetic geophysical data. We also discuss the implications of our results for the effective implementation of the EM algorithm for parameter estimation. Additionally, we provide a discussion on the relationships with existing results found in the literature. In particular, we show that our results converge to the results given in [13] for the one-dimensional case. Early detection is crucial for effectively treating skin cancer. Doctors rely on biopsies for an accurate diagnosis, but these procedures are invasive and pose risks to patients, so it's vital to develop a precise method for diagnosing skin cancer using non-invasive means, such as imaging techniques. In this study, a novel algorithm is presented to determine whether a biopsy is necessary for a particular skin growth based on a small image sample. The proposed method consists of two main components. Firstly, a deep learning technique is used to classify the image as normal or cancerous. However, since such networks can produce unreliable results due to their complex nature, the standard approach is modified to include the calculation of entropy alongside the classification output. This entropy measurement helps to identify image classifications that are likely incorrect. A clinical trial is conducted with a trained network using images from the PHIPedia dataset, and its effectiveness is validated in a real-world setting. The proposed algorithm is then applied to classify a skin growth as normal or cancerous, or to flag it as an outlier that requires further biopsy confirmation. The results show that this method delivers a high level of accuracy in both image classification and biopsies required, as validated across multiple datasets. The proposed algorithm is straightforward to implement and does not necessitate any additional training parameters. Furthermore, the findings are substantiated by comparing the proposed method against established deep learning techniques, both numerically and graphically. The proposed algorithm is subsequently made available online for public access. The study also presents several derivative applications of the proposed method, including but not limited to, analysis of existing dermatological image classification datasets, real-time skin cancer diagnosis using a single image, and combining the algorithm with surgical instruments to guide removal of cancerous tissues during surgery. The proposed method has significant potential uses in these areas once further development is completed. The results of the study are also plotted and graphed for easier understanding. The proposed algorithm is highly suitable for use in real-world settings due to its simplicity and accuracy. The study concludes by outlining several future research directions for the proposed method, including but not limited to, incorporation of spatial image information, integration with surgical instruments, and analysis of publicly available image classification datasets. In neural machine translation, the focus is typically set at the source sentence's token level to enable the decoder to selectively pay attention to specific source tokens when generating the target sentence. However, this approach has a crucial limitation: it restricts the decoder's attention to the immediately preceding source token, preventing it from considering future source tokens that may be more relevant to the target sentence's generation. To address this constraint, we introduce a novel look-ahead focus mechanism that permits the decoder to freely access all source tokens, including those located further away. This mechanism's implementation involves incorporating a set of target tokens that the decoder can freely sample from, which are then used to guide the decoder's attention towards more relevant source tokens based on their alignment. We evaluate this proposed look-ahead focus mechanism on real data, incorporating it into a state-of-the-art translation model that outperforms baseline models in various settings. This research demonstrates that granting the decoder freedom to explore different target tokens to focus on can lead to improved translation performance. Moreover, we show that our proposed look-ahead focus mechanism can be integrated into existing state-of-the-art models with a simple modification, requiring no additional training data. This approach's simplicity makes it appealing, with possible applications extending beyond neural machine translation. This research also introduces a new method for analyzing the decoder's attention over the target sentence, offering insights into the look-ahead focus mechanism's working. This analysis reveals that the majority of source tokens are infused with a weak, uniform importance that is constant across all target sentences, while a smaller subset of source tokens is associated with a stronger, sentence-specific importance. This finding's implications are then discussed in the paper. This research on the look-ahead focus mechanism also involves an in-depth examination of its relationship with existing approaches, including models that condition on the target sentence, bottom-up translation models, and approaches that incorporate external knowledge about the target sentence. This research on the look-ahead focus mechanism has the potential to contribute to both neural machine translation and related areas of research, including natural language generation and dialogue systems. We create two variants of multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis, one for uniform data dimensions and another for data with varying dimensional characteristics. The latter version's algorithm incorporates a new procedure for time-series data set alignment. Both methods' implementations are provided for practical application purposes. The introduced variants' performance is evaluated in a real-world application involving multivariate river flow patterns. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Notwithstanding its potential, accurate deformation measurement remains its primary challenge. This issue is compounded for elastography using focused ultrasound arrays, which measure deformation through the detection of changes in backscatter signals. As focused arrays inherently produce side lobes that generate unwanted data and necessitate complicated signal processing, they have largely been displaced by elastography systems using phased arrays, despite these arrays overestimate deformation due to the inaccurate detection of backscatter signals within their focal region. This paper introduces the Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) technique to dimensionally accurate elastography using focused arrays. This novel approach leverages signal processing to eliminate side lobes and side lobe data, thereby reducing beamforming aperture and overestimated deformation. Densely packed focused arrays provide the necessary data for this technique, which would otherwise require an excessively large phased array to produce accurate and comparable results. This approach has been tested using phantom data and validated with corresponding histological sections. These findings demonstrate the VSSA technique's effectiveness in reducing beamforming aperture, overestimated deformation and compound scattering-induced noise in elastography using focused arrays. This technique has the potential to transform elastography using focused arrays, with applications ranging from transvaginal and transrectal elastography to point elastography. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. However, when
tasks are dissimilar and aren't well connected, using shared representations can
lead to a problem called catastrophic interference, causing a learner to
struggle with multiple tasks. In our research, we discovered that reinforcement
learning agents using model-based methods can learn isolated networks for each
task, which greatly reduce the problem of categorical interference. We created
a variety of experiments, both theoretically and practically, to validate this
finding and showed that even when tasks are randomly generated, isolated
networks can still reduce the problem of categorical interference. We also
introduced a new way of calculating the difficulty of tasks based on graph
theory and found that tasks that are difficult for model-based agents are also
hard for connection-based methods. We were able to reduce the problem of
catastrophic interference to a question about graph theory and offered both
theoretical and practical evidence that challenges a commonly held assumption. 
We believe this could have implications for other areas of research outside 
multi-task reinforcement learning.

We create a formal system whose theories mirror the lifestyles of its four creators. This system is designed to ascertain how logicians live in a world where formal systems govern truth-telling. We then examine the world defined by this system for its inherent consistency, discovering that it isn't fundamentally consistent. In response, we modify the system to make its world more consistent, albeit at the cost of making truth a relative concept. Ultimately, we show that even with this adjustment, the system cannot be considered fundamentally reliable in defining what is true. This finding leads us to contemplate the implications for the practice of logic-based world-building. Additionally, we offer a concise proof of a previously known but formerly unpublished result regarding the system's reliability. Lastly, we conclude by examining the system's connection to a specific problem known as the "Godel world problem." This problem, first posed by Godel, asks if it's possible to create a formal system that accurately represents a world where arithmetic facts are universally known. We demonstrate that even with the system we've developed, it's impossible to create such a system for a specific, narrowly defined "Godel world." This system has the added benefit of allowing us to explore the concept of a world where arithmetic facts aren't universally known. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on capturing all possible posterior images and their associated probabilities. This research focuses on estimating the posterior distribution of images given the available data and certain prior constraints by using a regularized conditional GAN framework. This article examines a specific type of surface, invariant in nature, within a fractional-order dynamical system. To define this surface, it must satisfy a particular equation that is derived from the system's dynamics. By employing a specific approach, we investigate how the system's parameters influence the surface's existence. The article's main finding is that, due to the unique characteristics of fractional-order systems, there are specific system configurations for which no invariant surfaces can exist. The research further delves into the mathematical representation of these systems without invariant surfaces and provides an analytical solution to the surface equation. As a result, the article contributes an novel surface invariant concept to fractional-order dynamical systems. The associated proof offers a new approach to tackle surface invariance problems by leveraging the system's characteristics and exploring the connection between the surface and system dimensions. The article's main results are illustrated through numerical simulations of a real-world application. The research into surface invariance is further expanded to include the corresponding Lyapunov function, which in turn facilitates the analysis of the system's stability. The interstellar scintillation of pulsars can be used to study the properties of the interstellar medium. By analyzing the fluctuations in a pulsar's signal, researchers can decode the propagation path the signal took through the cosmos. Pulsar B1133+16, with its exceptionally strong signal, allows for a precise examination of the interstellar medium in the solar system's vicinity. Our data reveal the properties of the plasmatic component of the interstellar medium within the line of sight to the pulsar. This particular line of sight appears to be relatively clear of the solar system's plasma. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the properties of the plasmatic component remain essentially unchanged over time scales of a few years. Lastly, our analysis yields insights into the characteristics of the solar system's plasma within the Cygnus X region. This includes the discovery of a localized "anomaly" of high-electron-density plasma moving towards the Sun. This "anomaly" is distinct from the general plasma properties found in the surrounding interstellar space. To fully understand this phenomenon, additional observations are necessary to confirm this finding and investigate the properties of this peculiar plasma entity. If confirmed, it would mark the first discovery of a high-density plasma entity within the solar system's vicinity. To date, the solar system's vicinity has only been found to contain a diffuse high-density plasma within the Orion arm. This finding would reveal new aspects of the solar system's environment and shed light on the structure and dynamics of the local interstellar medium. To achieve this, it is essential to extend the time frame of the observations to gain a more comprehensive understanding of this "anomaly" and the surrounding interstellar medium. This would involve conducting regular scintillometry observations of the pulsar B1133+16 over a prolonged period. If carried out, this would yield a unique dataset with implications for the study of the solar system's environment and the local interstellar medium within the Cygnus X region. This study is part of a larger project dedicated to monitoring the interstellar medium within the solar system. This project involves conducting regular scintillometry observations of a group of pulsars with lines of sight to the solar system that are relatively clear of the solar system's plasma. To date, this project has discovered a previously unknown high-density plasma entity within the solar system's vicinity. To further explore the local interstellar medium within the Cygnus X region, it is essential to develop a comprehensive model of the plasmatic component of the interstellar medium

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through a pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural network. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using an autoregressive approach with vast exponential decay stacked (EDS) structures, offering real-time inference performance. However, the lack of memory in the EDS layers is thought to result in WN's limited pitch control capabilities. We hypothesize that incorporating memory in these layers could significantly improve pitch control. To validate this assumption, we developed a prototype based on the EDS layers with external memory, referring to it as the pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural network. Subsequent analysis revealed that QPNet's performance could be further enhanced by integrating the pitch-dependent expanded network at multiple levels, resulting in the QPNet model presented. Evaluations using the LJC corpus demonstrated improved pitch control in QPNet, while experiments using the NSynth dataset showed that the model could be switched between two distinct profiles to generate high-quality samples with diverse attributes. Our primary goal in this research was to create a challenging localization task for models that process visual information. To achieve this, we developed a method called "Non-Visual Noises" which adds Gaussian noise to higher-level representations of images, rather than their raw pixel data. We find that this type of noise is particularly difficult to overcome because it requires models to localize noise even after they have been processed and integrated with prior knowledge, a feature that distinguishes it from traditional noise localizations tasks. By incorporating this task into a standard deep learning framework, we were able to demonstrate that models that perform well on typical localization benchmarks often struggle with noises of this new type. Furthermore, this challenge can be utilized to gain insight into how models represent high-level visual information, and we show that it is effective in distinguishing between different model representations. Ultimately, this research provides a starting point for a novel line of inquiry that can be applied to a wide range of visual noise tasks. We open-source all data, code, and models associated with this project.

Recent advancements in large-scale graph data processing have led to a growing interest in graph neural networks, which have been successfully applied in various tasks including node classification, link prediction, and molecular design. However, existing GNN models have been trained primarily on large data sets with simple labelings. In contrast, many real-world problems involve complex and uncertain data, necessitating the development of robust methods to handle open-set and meta-learning scenarios. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel GNN architecture, named Lorentzian GNN (LGNN), that builds on the principles of Lorentzian geometry to provide a robust framework for learning on uncertain and dynamic graphs. By leveraging LGNN, we are able to reformulate key GNN operations using the Lorentzian metric, and demonstrate its effectiveness on a range of tasks including open-reconnaissance, in both transductive and semi-supervised settings. Furthermore, LGNN is able to outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in both synthetic and real-world experiments. Moreover, we show that LGNN is able to learn from meta-tasks by introducing a dynamic Lorentzian metric, and provide a theoretical analysis of its convergence properties. Lastly, we provide LGNN as a scalable open-source framework for large-scale learning on uncertain graphs. Code is available at: https://github.com/salestock/LGNN.
